messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rangi Parata is a 67-year-old widowed New Zealand-born Māori man who relocated to the United States two decades ago, building a quiet but respected career as an interior designer in Portland, Oregon. He is soft-spoken, precise in his aesthetic sensibilities, and was, until approximately fourteen months ago, known among colleagues for his calm presence on chaotic job sites. He first presented to the clinic following a referral from his GP, who had grown concerned after Rangi cancelled three consecutive check-up appointments and disclosed, almost in passing, that he had not been sleeping properly since returning from an overseas trip.

The trip had been both professional and personal. Rangi had accepted a commission to consult on a boutique hotel renovation in a North African city, work he had pursued partly as a distraction in the third year of his widowhood. On his fourth day there, he was detained at an unofficial checkpoint while travelling by car through a district his local contact had assured him was safe. The men who stopped the vehicle were armed, and Rangi was separated from his driver and held in a windowless storage room attached to a commercial building. He was kept there for approximately thirty-one hours. Throughout the ordeal, his captors moved in and out of the space, issuing instructions and arguing amongst themselves in Arabic, their voices rising and falling through the locked door and through the thin wall against which he sat on the floor, his back pressed to the concrete because it was the only position that allowed him to see the single entrance. He was released without physical injury after what he later learned was a ransom negotiation conducted by the hotel's management company. He flew home within forty-eight hours and told almost no one what had happened.

In the weeks that followed, Rangi found that the experience had rearranged something fundamental in how the world felt to him. Sounds were the most immediate intrusion. Arabic spoken anywhere — on a podcast, in a restaurant, from a passing conversation on the street — would produce a sudden, total return of the room: the smell of damp concrete, the quality of the light under the door, the sensation of his own breathing becoming deliberate and effortful. The memory did not arrive gradually; it arrived whole and without invitation. When he later tried to describe these episodes to his GP, he found he could not sustain the account. He would begin, lose the thread entirely, and sit in silence, not from reluctance but from a genuine inability to locate the sequence. At other times he could recite the facts of the detention in a flat, methodical voice, as though reading from someone else's file, feeling nothing at all — which disturbed him in a different way, as if the person in that room had not quite been him.

What had come to feel most dangerous to Rangi was the state of emotional vulnerability itself. When strong feeling arose — grief for his wife, frustration at a client, even pleasure at a finished room — his body would respond before he had formed any conscious thought: his pulse would accelerate, his shoulders would draw up, and he would be scanning the space around him for exits. He had come to believe that feeling anything intensely was itself a form of exposure, a lowering of guard he could not afford. He began rehearsing conversations before making any phone call or attending any meeting, constructing exact scripts so that nothing unexpected could be said to him. He stopped taking on projects that required site visits to buildings mid-renovation, because the enclosed corridors and locked staging areas were intolerable. By the eighth month, he had stopped going to his studio altogether, conducting what little work remained entirely by email, his output reduced to a fraction of its former volume. Two long-standing clients quietly moved on. A junior designer he had mentored for three years sent a concerned message that went unanswered for six weeks.

Rangi presented to the clinic following a conversation with his adult daughter in Auckland, who had noticed during a video call that he was sitting with his chair pushed against the wall of his own living room. He told her it helped him think. She did not press him then, but called again the following week. What brought him finally to seek help was not the lost clients or the shrinking world, but the fear that he was becoming unrecognisable to himself — and the fragile, uncertain hope that the person he had been before that room might not be entirely gone.
